summary: Gives guidance on reports about interoperation and implementation needed to advance a protocol to Draft Standard. It updates the earlier process because past reports varied widely in form. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a protocol gets promoted, people must show it works across programs. This tells them how to write that proof.

questions: how to advance to draft standard
what must an interoperability report contain
what is the ietf draft standard requirement
subtitle: How to write an implementation report that proves a protocol is ready for Draft Standard, with less paperwork.

tldr.problem: Advancing a protocol to Draft Standard requires a report on interoperation and implementation, but past reports varied widely in form and detail and new authors had little guidance.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5657 says what a report must contain, suggests a simple outline, relaxes some RFC 2026 requirements, and covers special cases such as deployed protocols, schemas and test suites.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 2026. The goal is a report that convinces the IETF and the IESG with just enough detail.

sections.title: Why Reports Need Guidance
sections.content:
Under RFC 2026, advancing to Draft Standard needs more than two interoperating implementations. The working group chair must also document the implementations and how their interoperation was tested, and send that to the Area Director with the protocol action request.

RFC 5657 says the barriers to advancing seem high or confusing. Reports accepted in the past varied widely. One example that is not enough, quoted in full, is a bare list of company names. It does not say how anyone knows the implementations interoperate. Other reports describe the test method at length but say little about what worked and what failed.

The primary goal is to convince the IETF and the IESG that the protocol is ready for Draft Standard, using a summary of interoperability and just enough detail to support it. The memo does not rule out good ideas, and the IESG uses judgement when a situation differs from what is described.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old proof-of-work notes were just a list of names, or a mountain of details with no result. This guide says what a good note looks like.

sections.title: What a Report Must Contain
sections.content:
The report MUST identify its author, who is responsible for characterizing the interoperability quality. It MAY name other contributors and reviewers, or name an active working group that reviewed it.

RFC 5657 relaxes several RFC 2026 requirements:

  • The report MAY name exactly which implementations were tested, though doing so usually helps.
  • The author MAY pick a level of detail for features rather than document each one.
  • A contributor other than a working group chair MAY submit the report to an Area Director.
  • Optional features that are not implemented, but are important and do not harm interoperability, MAY, exceptionally and with IESG approval, stay in a protocol at Draft Standard.

Independent implementations should be written by different people at different organizations using different code and protocol libraries. If there are only two implementations of an undeployed protocol, the report SHOULD identify them and their genealogy. A report also need not list every MAY, SHOULD and MUST in a full matrix.
sections.plainLanguage: You must say who wrote the report. You do not have to list every tiny detail, as long as you show the big picture is solid.

sections.title: Format and Suggested Outline
sections.content:
A report MUST be ASCII text with line breaks for readability, and no 8-bit characters are allowed. It may be formatted as an Internet-Draft but need not be. Titles are strongly RECOMMENDED to contain one or more RFC numbers for consistent lookup.

The outline, which a report MAY follow in part or in full, has these parts:

  • Title and Author.
  • Summary: attest that the standard meets the Draft Standard requirements, say how many implementations were tested or surveyed, characterize deployment, and call out difficult features.
  • Methodology: how the information was obtained, no longer than the summary.
  • Exceptions: any features thought to be problematic and why they do not disqualify the protocol.
  • Detail sections: background, such as how security, internationalization, management and IANA registrations worked out.
  • Appendix sections: optional test material that may help follow-on reports and new implementors.
sections.plainLanguage: The report is like a short school project with a title, a summary, how you checked, what went wrong, and extra notes at the back.

sections.title: Choosing the Level of Feature Detail
sections.content:
What counts as a feature has been frequently debated. A report written at too high a level cannot be verified and may miss a real failure to interoperate. One written at too fine a level produces an exploding matrix of requirement interactions that buries the important points.

The best reports use a level of detail just enough to convince the reader that testing covered the requirements and would have found any gap. The RFC points to the report for RTP/RTCP as a model, with numbered items marked PASS or FAIL, each with a short note on which implementations were tested. It prefers this to an exhaustive checklist of every normative statement. Working group consensus that a report covers the specification can also be a strong statement.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not say only 'it works' and do not write a book. Give enough checks that a skeptic would be satisfied.

sections.title: Special Cases
sections.content:
Deployed protocols: laboratory results matter less than what works in deployment, so surveying implementors or operators can be more informative. Finding problems is more useful than gathering long feature checklists.

Undeployed protocols: finer-grained detail is appropriate, and reports should anticipate operational concerns such as overload or congestion management.

Schemas, languages and formats: the IESG SHOULD use judgement. ABNF is given as an example, where real RFCs that use it serve as implementations, and MIB modules are another.

Multiple contributors: reports per implementation MAY be submitted one by one and SHOULD be collated into one document for archiving.

Test suites: automated tests can be built from real-world examples. The Litmus client for WebDAV is a counter-example, since it tests server completeness and simple cases, not real-world use.

Optional and extensibility features: an optional feature must still be implemented somewhere by more than one independent implementation, or the report must say so and explain why the feature must stay. A version field in a first release is a typical case.
sections.plainLanguage: Different things get checked in different ways. A toy that kids already play with gets a survey of players, and a brand new toy gets a careful test.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC offers two. The first is a minimal report for SMTP pipelining, which lists several SMTP implementations that support it and notes no reported interoperability problems. The RFC says the different vendors and platforms imply the codebases are by and large independent, and that the report would only be slightly improved by saying who provided the summary and that problems were actively asked about.

The second covers exceptions. In an SMTP implementation survey, the VRFY and EXPN commands were often not implemented or disabled. A good exceptions section would explain that this does not hurt interoperability, since EXPN is optional and VRFY can get a non-response, and that the commands remain useful to administrators in controlled circumstances.
sections.plainLanguage: Two sample notes show the idea: one short note for something that worked everywhere, and one that explains why a few rarely used buttons do not matter.

items.title: Summary
items.text: Attests the standard meets Draft Standard requirements and says how many implementations were tested.

items.title: Methodology
items.text: How the information was obtained; no longer than the summary.

items.title: Exceptions
items.text: Problematic features and why they do not disqualify the protocol.

items.title: Detail sections
items.text: Background such as security, internationalization and IANA experience.
